title: Doodling

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When someone feels a little bored in a long meeting, or while waiting on the telephone, they may take their pen and doodle. Next time you do this, look at what appears on the pad – you may be surprised by what you see. Doodling is a less conscious process than handwriting, and the results tend to be far more varied and individual, ranging from the highly ornate to the banal. Some symbols appear again and again – little houses, cars, flowers, birds, arrows, stars, numbers and names are especially common. But why do we doodle? It may be that it is nothing more than a form of fidgeting – something to do when bored, or waiting for something to happen. However, it can also be used for a number of practical purposes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Although decorating paper with squiggles, scribbles and little drawings may simply be harmless stress relief, it may also be more than that. Psychologist Dr Ho Law claims that doodling is a creative activity, coming from the right side of the brain. He uses it extensively in his work with clients. Ingrid Collins, a London-based therapist, believes that doodling is an important warm-up exercise for artists. ‘It can be likened to a singer warming up for a performance by singing scales,’ she says. ‘A blank canvas can be very daunting, and doodling is a good way of getting started.’ There is also evidence that doodling can prepare the brain for mental activity. Dr Wendy Van Dyk of Dort College, Indiana, asked students to take notes, or to doodle, or just to listen during lectures. When tested to see how much they had taken in, the note-takers and doodlers scored the same, doing significantly better than the listeners.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some psychologists consider that doodling is a visual form of daydreaming. According to Professor Robert Harrison of Boston University, people indulge in three kinds of daydreaming – wish-fulfilment, worrying and planning ahead. He believes that doodles usually have something to do with pleasurable wish-fulfilment. For instance, if planes appear in doodles, they may express a longing to escape from it all. Other psychologists claim that doodling can give an insight into the personality of the doodler.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Like handwriting, doodling is sometimes analysed to give clues to the personality, although it must be said that handwriting analysis, known as graphology, is not universally accepted in the world of psychology. Those who do accept it agree that the details of a doodle are dependent on a person’s cultural background and education. Handwriting is analysed by the size, shape and spacing of the letters; with doodles, it is the symbols and pictures that are important. ‘You can read a doodle like a book,’ says Dr Ho. ‘Doodling is a creative outlet that reflects a person’s state of mind.’

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Graphologist Peter West claims that upward pointing arrows can represent a desire to succeed, for example, while arrows pointing in all directions may indicate an open mind. A person who doodles straight lines is often a blunt person who speaks his or her mind; noughts and crosses in a doodle may indicate a competitive person, and perfectionists may draw stars. Some people rarely doodle; Dr West describes them as ‘precise, direct and controlled.’

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many therapists use doodling in their work with clients. According to Ingrid Collins, ‘Art can play an immense role in therapy, because psychology and art, from spontaneous doodling to great works, are closely connected.’ When analysing a doodle, she looks for signs, such as whether the drawing covers the entire page or just a small corner, whether it is fluid and flexible or rigid and tight. A good starting point, she says, is to have the client doodle for a while, first to relax them and then to create a starting point for dialogue, with the therapist asking the client to talk about what they have drawn.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Many therapists use doodling in their work with clients. According to Ingrid Collins, ‘Art can play an immense role in therapy, because psychology and art, from spontaneous doodling to great works, are closely connected.’ When analysing a doodle, she looks for signs, such as whether the drawing covers the entire page or just a small corner, whether it is fluid and flexible or rigid and tight. A good starting point, she says, is to have the client doodle for a while, first to relax them and then to create a starting point for dialogue, with the therapist asking the client to talk about what they have drawn.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Anyone can experiment with the use of drawing to enable them to think more creatively or to brainstorm ideas. Using stick figures and faces, symbols and signs, letters and words to depict whatever is happening in the mind, it may be possible to reach a creative breakthrough. Even those who are more accustomed to writing may wish to try doodling in order to rediscover their creativity. Artist Corinne Pratz recommends doodling as a problem-solving technique. She suggests starting with a stick person and then doodling around it, using symbols, names and signs to indicate the situation; then she recommends that the paper should be set aside for a while. When the doodler looks at it again, she says, new answers and ideas may appear.
